sources.title: Chinese: A Linguistic Introduction excerpt
sources.note: Introduces Chinese as a Sino-Tibetan language and distinguishes modern varieties from the earliest written records.

sources.title: Joseph Edkins and the reconstruction of Early Chinese
sources.note: Explains that reconstructed Early or Old Chinese sound classes are scholarly models rather than directly recorded speech.

sources.title: The evidence for Old Chinese
sources.note: Describes how later rhyme books, phonetic series, early inscriptions and comparative evidence contribute to Old Chinese reconstruction.

sources.title: Phylogenetic evidence for Sino-Tibetan origin in northern China
sources.note: Bayesian lexical model supports one northern-origin scenario while retaining large time ranges and model dependence.

sources.title: Ancient genomes from northern China and subsistence change
sources.note: Fifty-five ancient genomes reveal changing Yellow, West Liao and Amur-region ancestry and complex links with subsistence.

sources.title: Ancient genomes reveal demographic history of coastal southern China
sources.note: Ancient genomic study documents layered southern population histories and later farmer movements rather than one timeless ancestry.

sources.title: Chinese writing
sources.note: Places the earliest fully developed Chinese writing in late Shang oracle-bone inscriptions and notes that its immediate predecessors remain unclear.

sources.title: The Chinese language and writing system
sources.note: Locates the earliest Chinese language evidence at late Shang Anyang and describes the royal divination archive.

sources.title: Chinese oracle-bone inscriptions
sources.note: Institutional record identifies the Yin ruins at Anyang and dates the Shang divination archive broadly to 1400 to 1100 BCE.

sources.title: Radiocarbon dating of Late Shang oracle bones
sources.note: Explains oracle-bone discovery, corpus, royal context, decipherment and chronological methods.

sources.title: Ancient Central China
sources.note: Regional synthesis of Middle Yangzi landscapes, salt, settlements, political centers and networked peripheries.

sources.title: The Middle Yangzi: archaeology and history of Chu and its predecessors
sources.note: Separates Chu as polity, region, identity and archaeological label and traces its late Western Zhou development.

sources.title: Tanheli Site archaeological protection profile
sources.note: Hunan provincial cultural authorities describe Tanheli as a protected Bronze Age site with pottery, bronze and jade finds, grounding the localized comparison.

sources.title: Archaeology of the Chinese Bronze Age: From Erlitou to Anyang
sources.note: UCLA archaeological synthesis places Central Plains centers within distinct interaction zones reaching the Yangzi, steppe, Tibetan Plateau and Gansu corridor.

sources.title: Formation of early states: Erlitou and Erligang
sources.note: Central Plain chronology, urbanism, bronze production and Erligang expansion used as a neighbor comparison.

sources.title: Shang archaeology
sources.note: History and archaeology of Shang centers, Anyang and regional material connections.

sources.title: Anyang and beyond: Shang and contemporary Bronze Age cultures
sources.note: Contrasts the Anyang metropolis with contemporary regional Bronze Age societies.

sources.title: Bronze Age metal circulation in China
sources.note: Lead-isotope and compositional approaches investigate ore and metal movement while emphasizing interpretive limits.

sources.title: Indigenous production and interregional exchange in the Hanzhong basin
sources.note: Technical study of more than seven hundred late-second-millennium bronzes identifies both local production and interregional links.

sources.title: Tonglushan Ancient Copper Mine Sites
sources.note: Institutional description of timbered shafts, smelting remains and mining tools beginning in the eleventh century BCE.

sources.title: Rediscovery of Zeng and interregional networks
sources.note: Excavated inscribed bronzes recover Zeng history, kin ties, elite cemeteries and metal networks in Hubei.

sources.title: Western Zhou archaeology
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis of settlements, burials and inscribed ritual bronzes in the Western Zhou world.

sources.title: The Bronze Age economy, 1045 to 707 BCE
sources.note: Discusses resource mobilization, ritual bronzes, political institutions and the elite bias of surviving evidence.

sources.title: Sanzuodian fortified settlements in northeast China
sources.note: Survey and architectural analysis of Lower Xiajiadian stone walls, towers, round houses and labor investment.

sources.title: Ancient DNA from a Lower Xiajiadian population
sources.note: Small uniparental-marker study of fourteen Dadianzi individuals illustrates both mobility signals and severe sampling limits.

sources.title: Bronze cultures of the northern frontiers
sources.note: Survey of northern and northwestern metallurgical, pastoral and exchange traditions beyond Central Plain narratives.

sources.title: China and the steppe: reception and resistance
sources.note: Tracks selective adoption and transformation of horses, chariots and metal technologies through frontier interaction.

sources.title: Settlement pattern study in northeast China
sources.note: Regional survey demonstrates how systematic settlement data test culture-history assumptions in northeast China.

sources.title: The origins and dispersal of rice cultivation
sources.note: Archaeobotanical review of rice cultivation and dispersal along the Yangzi and beyond.

sources.title: Variation of millet grain size and cooking techniques across Asia
sources.note: Comparative archaeobotany connects grain traits with regional boiling, steaming, grinding and baking traditions.

sources.title: Stable isotopes and dental caries in ancient China
sources.note: Isotope and dental data trace broad dietary change while showing limits of pooled, uneven samples.

sources.title: Ancient human parasites in Chinese populations
sources.note: Paleoparasitology review includes later Hubei mummies and a Han latrine, providing comparison and evidence limits.

sources.title: Production insights into jade, bronze, and turquoise Shang ceremonial weapons
sources.note: Smithsonian technical study uses microscopy, radiography and manufacturing traces to reconstruct casting, drilling, assembly and polishing sequences.

sources.title: The Origins of Chinese Writing
sources.note: Oxford archaeological synthesis distinguishes mature late-Shang writing from earlier regional sign systems whose relationship to speech remains debated.

sources.title: But is it History of Medicine? Twenty Years in the History of the Healing Arts of China
sources.note: Scholarly review locates securely contextualized early medical manuscripts mainly near the dawn of empire and stresses material context, diverse healing and dating limits.

sources.title: The Stage: Daily Life in Ancient China
sources.note: Explains the elite and ritual bias of bronze and tomb evidence and its relationship to social status.

sources.title: What elites wore in 500 to 300 BCE China
sources.note: Traces designs between textiles, bamboo and bronzes; later preserved cloth helps interpret earlier patterns cautiously.

sources.title: Migration in Bronze Age southern China: elite Chu burials
sources.note: Integrates isotopes, genetics and archaeology for later Chu elites, useful as an explicitly later methodological comparison.

sources.title: Panlongcheng 2024 archaeological field school
sources.note: Institutional field report describes modern excavation training and the site’s walls, palatial foundations, tombs, workshops and artifacts.

proposedOverrides.summary: A cautious guide to the many Bronze and early Iron Age communities placed under the atlas’s “Sinic” umbrella, separating language reconstruction from archaeology while exploring farms, mines, homes, families, health, writing limits and continuity from 1500 to 500 BCE.
